clinicalPearls: Acute self-limited vasculitis of childhood, mainly under age 5, that preferentially targets medium-sized arteries, especially the coronary arteries.

Classic diagnosis needs fever for five or more days plus four of five criteria: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes (cracked lips, strawberry tongue), polymorphous rash, extremity changes (edema, erythema, later periungual desquamation), and cervical lymphadenopathy usually unilateral and over 1.5 cm.
Incomplete (atypical) presentations are common in infants under 6 months and older children, and this group carries a higher, not lower, risk of coronary aneurysm.
Irritability out of proportion to exam findings and marked perineal desquamation in the diaper area are supportive clues.
Untreated disease leads to coronary artery aneurysms in roughly a quarter of children; timely therapy sharply reduces this risk.
Think of Kawasaki disease in any young febrile child with unexplained sterile pyuria, gallbladder hydrops, or aseptic meningitis.
Highest risk of coronary aneurysm formation is in the subacute phase, roughly one to four weeks after fever onset, coinciding with marked thrombocytosis.
harrison.pathophysiology: Kawasaki disease is thought to arise from an exaggerated innate and adaptive immune response, possibly triggered by an unidentified infectious agent, in a genetically susceptible host. The resulting medium-vessel vasculitis targets the coronary arteries, causing panvasculitis with destruction of the internal elastic lamina and media, which weakens the vessel wall and predisposes to aneurysm formation and later stenosis or thrombosis. Systemic inflammation also produces the mucocutaneous and lymph node findings that define the clinical syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Scarlet fever / group A streptococcal infection
Staphylococcal or streptococcal toxic shock syndrome
infectionMimics: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome / toxic shock syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiogram — baseline and serial imaging to detect coronary artery dilation or aneurysm
CBC with differential — leukocytosis early, thrombocytosis typically emerging in the subacute phase
ESR and CRP — markedly elevated, supports diagnosis and tracks inflammatory activity
Liver function tests — mild transaminitis and hypoalbuminemia are common
Urinalysis — sterile pyuria from urethritis supports the diagnosis
ECG — screen for arrhythmia or ischemic changes related to coronary involvement
Blood culture and throat culture — help exclude streptococcal and other bacterial mimics
Lipid panel — baseline assessment given long-term cardiovascular risk in those with aneurysms
redFlags: Evidence of coronary artery dilation or aneurysm on echocardiogram warrants urgent cardiology involvement
Signs of myocarditis, pericardial effusion, or hemodynamic instability (Kawasaki disease shock syndrome)
Persistent or recrudescent fever after initial therapy suggesting treatment resistance
Very young infants or children with incomplete presentations, who are at higher risk of coronary complications
Marked thrombocytosis in the subacute phase increasing thrombotic risk in dilated vessels
pitfalls: Dismissing the diagnosis because not all classic criteria are present, especially in infants who often have incomplete disease with greater cardiac risk
Delaying treatment while awaiting full criteria, since early therapy within the first ten days of fever meaningfully lowers aneurysm risk
Overlooking overlap with MIS-C in the appropriate epidemiologic context, which requires additional testing and different considerations
Failing to arrange long-term cardiology follow-up in children with documented coronary changes
harrison.prognosis: With prompt recognition and treatment most children recover fully with resolution of fever and inflammation within days. Coronary artery aneurysms, when they occur, may regress over time but can also persist, predisposing to late stenosis, thrombosis, or ischemic events, so children with cardiac involvement need long-term surveillance.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Vasculitis (Kawasaki Disease)
management: Give intravenous immunoglobulin with aspirin promptly, ideally early in the illness, to reduce the risk of coronary artery aneurysms
Continue aspirin at anti-inflammatory dosing during the acute phase, switching to antiplatelet dosing once fever settles
For immunoglobulin resistance, use a repeat immunoglobulin infusion, corticosteroids, or the TNF inhibitor infliximab
Intensify initial therapy with adjunctive corticosteroids in children at high risk of coronary complications
Add anticoagulation such as warfarin for large or giant coronary aneurysms to prevent thrombosis
Perform baseline and serial echocardiography to detect and monitor coronary artery dilation and aneurysm
Arrange long-term paediatric cardiology follow-up for children with persistent coronary involvement
